U.S. Highway 95 winds up White Bird hill in a series of sharp curves and a dozen switchbacks, giving the im- pression of a confused snake crawling up a hill. This eight-mile section of two-lane road was originally only sixteen feet wide but in 1938 was widened to eighteen feet. Most of the switchbacks are in a relatively small segment of the grade, so that anyone going along the road scarcely can tell whether the rest of the traffic is going in the same or in the opposite direction. A new grade which will replace the old route is all but complete, with only a bridge still to be built. When the new grade is finished, the old road will remain as a marvel of highway building during the early automobile era. The southern terminus for the White Bird grade is at a point m described as 45°46'40" latitude and 116°17'04" longitude; northern m terminus is at a point described as 45O52'28" latitude and 116°12'10" longitude. The corridor which follows the road between these two points is 60 feet wide. TO C n

The total cost of this first project was $362,155. The road was later surfaced with crushed rock in three separate projects in 1922, 1925 and 1927. Finally the road was surfaced with roadmix bituminous in two projects in 1937 and 1938, bringing the total cost for the 21.1 miles of road to $521,316. Highway 95 is the only highway in Idaho which connects the northern part of the state with the southern part. The White Bird hill is well-known by all who drive the road as a place where traffic slows considerably, even in good weather, to wind either up or down the sharp curves and switchbacks. Under bad weather conditions, White Bird hill presents a major obstacle to all north-south traffic. The new grade will be appreciated for its greater speed and safety, but the original White Bird grade will be remembered as one of the marvels of highway engineering, built when cars did not travel much more than 25 miles per hour. v ^/ 0 1974
